answer.rationale: Rollback is ruled out by compliance (security patch), which eliminates memory_b1's pattern regardless of how well it worked on day 18. That leaves failover, capacity, circuit breaker, and replica routing. The failure mode here is write-path p99, not dependency failure, so a circuit breaker (memory_b4) would shed exactly the settlement writes the objective says to preserve; add_capacity (memory_b3) was validated pre-emptively before a known peak and takes provisioning time we do not have 90 minutes into an active climb. memory_b2's regional failover is the tempting match because the degradation is region-confined, but that memory was consolidated as a latency win during a March degradation and says nothing about in-flight write durability under peak settlement load; a clean traffic shift for read-mostly latency is not evidence of a clean shift for heavy writes, and this is the one intervention where the downside is the specific thing we are told not to lose. memory_b5 is the closest structural match: it describes primary write latency recovering the same day after non-transactional read load was moved off the primary. That is the same mechanism available now, it is reversible, and it cannot drop customer writes. I want the archive records for memory_b2 and memory_b5 specifically to check (a) whether the March failover occurred under comparable write volume or during a low-write window, and (b) whether memory_b5's recovery was actually attributable to replica routing or coincided with an unrelated fix, since all six memories are consolidated success stories with no recorded failures or base rates. That one-sided survivorship in the inherited record is the main reason I am not treating any of these as settled. If memory_b5's causal attribution turns out to be weak, and memory_b2 shows write-safe failover under load, I would switch to regional_failover; if memory_b2 is silent on writes I hold replica routing this window and queue failover for the next.
